candidates.title: Metal-ion coordination drives active-site remodeling for backsplicing in circularly permuted group II introns
candidates.abstract: AbstractCircularly permuted (CP) group II introns are self-splicing ribozymes that undergo a sequential branching and backsplicing reaction to yield branched introns and circular exons (circRNAs). While the initial branching step is structurally characterized, the mechanistic principles that govern the subsequent large-scale active-site remodeling and stringent metal-ion specificity required for backsplicing remain poorly understood. Here, we present a series of high-resolution cryo-EM structures of the CP group II intron from Gluconacetobacter diazotrophicus PAL5 (Gdi-1), capturing the ribozyme at discrete stages along the branching -to- backsplicing pathway under distinct ionic conditions. Comparative analyses under K+/Mg2+, K+/Ca2+, and Cs+/Mg2+ conditions demonstrate that productive backsplicing relies on ion-specific coordination networks that govern 3′ splice site (3′SS) docking and catalytic center formation, revealing the precise metal-ion-coordinated conformational rearrangements and dynamic splice-site exchange mechanisms. Crucially, we identify a previously unrecognized, highly selective monovalent cation-binding site, K3, that structurally couples the γ–γ′ interaction to reassembly of the heteronuclear four-metal core, thereby promoting productive second-step active-site formation. Together, these findings establish a structural basis for metal-ion-dependent active-site remodeling during group II intron catalysis and provide mechanistic insights into metal-ion selectivity in circRNA biogenesis.

candidates.title: Bacterial sialidases subvert the complement system through desialylation
candidates.journal: Protein Science : A Publication of the Protein Society
candidates.authors: Kurniyati K, Clark N, Fu Q, Zhang S, Qiu W, Malkowski M, Li C.
candidates.abstract: AbstractBacterial sialidases (neuraminidases) are widely studied virulence factors, yet their impact on the complement system, a central component of innate immunity, remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the effects of six sialidases from five human pathogens, including Bacteroides fragilis, Clostridium perfringens, Tannerella forsythia, Treponema denticola, and Vibrio cholerae on complement immunity using an integrated approach combining genetics, biochemistry, glycobiology, mass spectrometry, and structural biology. We show that major complement proteins, including C1q, C4, and C5, as well as complement regulators Factor I, Factor H, and C4BP, are modified by terminal sialic acids (sialylation) and undergo terminal desialylation by all six sialidases. Using the oral pathogen T. denticola and its sialidase NanH as a representative model, we demonstrate that sialidase‐mediated desialylation suppresses complement activation and surface deposition, promoting complement evasion. Structural analyses of T. denticola NanH in complex with an inhibitor, sialic acid, and native glycans, together with comparisons to other sialidase structures, reveal the molecular basis of substrate recognition and catalysis. Despite substantial sequence diversity, all six exo‐α‐sialidases share a conserved six‐bladed β‐propeller catalytic domain and cleave both N‐acetylneuraminic acid and N‐glycolylneuraminic acid, the predominant mammalian sialic acids. Together, these findings establish a conserved structural and functional mechanism by which diverse bacterial pathogens desialylate complement components to impair innate immune defense.

candidates.title: Allosteric Communication in the Tubulin Dimer Revealed through Molecular Dynamics and Network Analysis
candidates.abstract: AbstractMicrotubules are dynamic polymers essential for intracellular organization, with basic constituents being αβ-tubulin dimers. Microtubule growth and shrinkage is tightly regulated by GTP hydrolysis in β-tubulin, yet how the information about the bound nucleotide propagates across the tubulin dimer, beyond its direct binding site, remains unclear. Here we combine extensive all-atom molecular dynamics simulations of αβ-tubulin dimers with GTP or GDP in the β-subunit to investigate longitudinal allosteric signaling. We featurize conformations using residue-wise minimum distances between the two subunits, apply EncoderMap dimensionality reduction and HDBSCAN clustering to identify conformational substates, and perform dynamic network analysis on these clusters. We find that the tubulin dimer relaxes from the straight starting structures into a broad ensemble of bent conformations, and that the bound nucleotide does not by itself separate this ensemble. The simulations retain a comparatively long-lived memory of their starting structure that makes the subtler nucleotide signal harder to detect. Network analysis identifies residues that are most important for information flow, as well as preferred communication routes across the longitudinal interface. Substate-specific analysis indicates that the transition from the GTP- to GDP-bound state is associated with changes in the preferred allosteric routes, enhancing our understanding of longitudinal communication in tubulin. Beyond tubulin, our approach illustrates how combining dimensionality reduction with substate-specific network analysis can uncover hidden allosteric signatures in protein assemblies.

candidates.authors: Dolgusheva V, Leibin I, Kudryashova N, Mukanov A, Kuznetsov I, Manasyan A, Pavlyuk G, Mishkorez I, Keremet A, Podlesnyi P, Kalinkin A, Avdeev K, Kuznetsov M, Parfenov N, Gromov S, Ufaev D, Nasaev S.
candidates.abstract: AbstractSystematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX)-based aptamer discovery can be constrained by target availability, selection biases, and optimization requirements. We introduce Xelari, a modular pipeline for de novo DNA and RNA aptamer design from protein structures without target-specific SELEX data or retraining. Xelari combines algorithmic modules with surrogate models trained on physical or structural references. InNA reproduced nucleotide-amino-acid interaction energies with RMSE of 0.19 kcal/mol across 483,735 reference pairs. AliNA achieved a mean F1 of 0.757 on 339 PDB-derived RNA evaluation sequences. Edgar correlated with experimental folding energies but did not reproduce their absolute scale, supporting its use as a ranking heuristic. Under the reported calibration, ValentiNA showed MAE of 0.931 kcal/mol and Spearman ρ of 0.795 across 32 retrospective records associated with 27 structural templates; this analysis does not establish family-independent validation. Prospectively, three DNA aptamers designed against Treponema pallidum protein structures showed cell-associated binding in a treponeme assay (apparent KD, 0.91–2.57 μM). A fourth DNA aptamer served as a capture reagent in a serum-based hybrid aptamer-antibody assay for Tau441. These applications support feasibility without establishing intended-target engagement in the cellular assay or a general success rate, positioning structure-based design as a complement to experimental selection.Keywords: MT: Special Issue: Innovations in Aptamer Technology, aptamer, de novodesign, SELEX-free, structure-based design, machine learning, binding affinity prediction, nucleic acid-protein interaction, nucleic acid secondary structure prediction, binding site prediction, folding free energy

candidates.title: Comparative Analysis of the Binding Characteristics of Fluorescein and Rhodamine B with Bovine Serum Albumin
candidates.authors: Afolabi S, Feoktistova V, Sbytov D, Novikov O, Botnar A, Ulasevich S, Skorb E, Shityakov S.
candidates.abstract: Bovine serum albumin (BSA) serves as a key model for investigating protein–ligand interactions and is crucial for understanding drug pharmacokinetics and developing biomedical probes. This study presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of the binding of fluorescein and rhodamine B to BSA, employing UV–vis absorption, fluorescence, molecular docking, and 1000 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. The results revealed competitive binding, with rhodamine B exhibiting a greater affinity (ΔG MMGBSA = −48.17 kcal/mol) than fluorescein (−23.16 kcal/mol), which was supported by fluorescence quenching and binding analyses. Molecular docking confirmed Sudlow’s site I as the primary binding site, whereas MD simulations highlighted stable complexes driven by van der Waals and electrostatic forces, particularly for rhodamine B. Unexpectedly, the superior affinity of rhodamine B under physiological pH deviates from lipophilic trends. These findings enhance the molecular understanding of dye–protein interactions, providing a robust basis for designing advanced fluorescent probes, drug conjugates, and diagnostic platforms.

candidates.title: Discovery and Design of YTHDF2-Selective and Pan-YTHDF Inhibitors for m6A Binding by the YTH Aromatic Cage
candidates.authors: Sikorski V, Salo J, Selberg S, Costa Sa D, Renzi B, Teino I, Blokhina D, Virtanen S, Antenucci L, Saarma M, Permi P, Karelson M, Kankuri E.
candidates.abstract: AbstractRecognition of N6-methyl-adenosine (m6A) in the RNA sequences by the YT521-B homology domain-containing protein family paralogs 1–3 (YTHDF1–3) is a dominant layer of myriad cellular regulation. Dysregulated YTHDF paralog expression and activities have been reported in cancer, including glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) in which YTHDF2 has been identified as a druggable dependency. Guided by structure-based in silico screening, we identified structurally related small-molecule compound families of promising YTHDF inhibitor compounds. Following in vitro screening, two hits, DT11 and DT15, emerged and were further examined. We identified DT11 as a YTHDF2-selective inhibitor of the YTH domain using proximity-based bead assays, microscale thermophoresis, molecular dynamics, and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. DT11 demonstrated 10–100-fold YTHDF2-selectivity (IC50: YTHDF2 16.6 μM; YTHDF1 185 μM; YTHDF3 1300 μM) in inhibiting m6A-RNA binding, whereas the pan-inhibitor DT15 effectively inhibited all the paralogs (IC50: YTHDF2 12.6 μM; YTHDF1 18.8 μM; YTHDF3 31 μM). In LN229 glioblastoma cells, DT11 reduced cell viability and showed relevant additive efficacy with the gold standard Temozolomide. DT15 blocked GBM cell invasion and scratch wound closure. Similar effects were observed after inhibition of the m6A writer METTL3 activity by STM2457. No such effects were observed with DT11. A minutely modified DT11 derivative, DT11-1, showed 10-fold increases in YTHDF2-selective m6A binding and LN229 cell viability inhibitory potencies. All the compounds produced high GBM preference over primary neurons and HEK293 cells in their effects. Our results further define pharmacological molecular comprehensions for paralog-dependent engagement of m6A in RNA by the aromatic cage for the selective modulation of YTHDF functions.

candidates.title: Lateral opening site of human oligopeptide transporter 2 plays a key role in the interaction with polymyxins
candidates.authors: Jiang X, Luo Y, Azad MAK, Xu L, Xiao M, Velkov T, Roberts KD, Thamlikitkul V, Zhou QT, Zhou F, Li J.
candidates.abstract: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) Gram-negative bacteria pose a critical global health threat, while polymyxins remain a last-line therapy. However, their clinical use is limited by nephrotoxicity. Human oligopeptide transporter 2 (hPepT2) is a membrane transporter mediating the reabsorption of polymyxins in renal cells and contributes to their nephrotoxicity, but the molecular basis of their interaction remains unclear. Here, we investigated the structure-interaction relationship (SIR) of polymyxins with hPepT2 by integrating computational, chemical, and cell biology approaches. Bioinformatic modeling predicted an outward-facing hPepT2 structure and a potential transport pathway, with polymyxins interacting at the lateral opening, particularly E214, D215, D317, D342, and E622. Transporter mutagenesis and molecular analyses confirmed that D215 is critical for polymyxin binding, while other residues influence transporter turnover and/or expression. We subsequently synthesized polymyxin analogs with modifications at Dab1, Dab3, Dab5, and Dab9 of polymyxins, which reduced interactions with hPepT2. Notably, alanine substitution at Dab3 reduced nephrotoxicity in mice while retaining antibacterial activity. Overall, this proof-of-concept study demonstrates that the hPepT2-polymyxin SIR model provides a viable strategy for developing novel, safer lipopeptide antibiotics.

candidates.authors: Hegazy M, Abbass H, Abouelela M, Mahmoud A, Hassanein M, Abdelmaksoud N, Ibrahim A, Al-Harrasi A, El-Hela A.
candidates.abstract: The study explored the metabolite profile and anticancer potential of Paspalum dilatatum (Dallis grass) using an integrated phytochemical, computational, and in vitro approach. UHPLC/QTOF-MS/MS analysis of a 70% methanolic extract tentatively identified 30 metabolites, mainly flavonoids. In vitro MTT assays showed dose-dependent cytotoxicity against breast cancer MCF7 cells (IC50 = 73.70 µg mL−1) and liver cancer HEPG2 cells (IC50 = 128.02 µg mL−1), with high selectivity over normal Vero cells (p < 0.0001). Mechanistic studies in MCF7 cells demonstrated apoptosis induction, as supported by increased caspase-3 expression (P = 0.0002). Upregulation of the pro-apoptotic protein BAX (P = 0.0013) and downregulation of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL-2 (P = 0.0284) were also demonstrated, with a significant rise in the BAX/BCL-2 ratio (P = 0.0060). Computational docking against EGFR (PDB ID: 8A27) predicted strong binding of acaciin (−9.763 kcal mol−1) and sissotrin (−9.587 kcal mol−1), while molecular dynamics supported the stability of the EGFR–Acaciin complex (RMSD 2.5–3 Å). Overall, the integrated findings position P. dilatatum flavonoids, and acaciin in particular, as computationally prioritized candidates for EGFR-targeted, pro-apoptotic anticancer activity that merit further experimental validation.

candidates.title: Purpurin Alleviates Meniscal Senescence and Osteoarthritis by Blocking the Non‐Metabolic Function of Hexokinase 2
candidates.authors: Lin Z, Li M, Li W, Xu T, Jiang Z, Zhong Y, He A, Zhao X, Long D, Kang Y.
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTMeniscal degeneration, characterised by extracellular matrix (ECM) loss and cellular senescence, plays a critical role in osteoarthritis (OA) progression, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Although hexokinase 2 (HK2) is recognised as a key glycolytic enzyme, its potential non‐metabolic functions in the meniscus remain unexplored. In this study, HK2 expression was evaluated in human OA and normal meniscus tissues, and its non‐metabolic effects were investigated in primary meniscal cells using overexpression, knockdown, and site‐directed mutagenesis; protein interactions were analysed by immunoprecipitation‐mass spectrometry (IP‐MS) and co‐immunoprecipitation (Co‐IP). HK2 was significantly upregulated in OA meniscal tissues, and overexpression of catalytically inactive HK2 promoted meniscal ECM degradation and cellular senescence in an MYH10‐dependent manner. Mechanistically, HK2 enhanced the MYH10–PRKN interaction, inducing K48‐linked ubiquitination of MYH10 at lysine 410 and its subsequent proteasomal degradation, thereby reducing COL1A1 mRNA stability. Purpurin, identified through virtual screening, disrupted the HK2–MYH10 interaction in vitro, prevented MYH10 degradation, and attenuated cellular senescence. In the destabilisation of the medial meniscus (DMM) mouse model, intra‐articular injection of adeno‐associated virus expressing catalytically inactive HK2 exacerbated OA progression, whereas purpurin treatment alleviated meniscal degeneration, ECM loss, and OA‐associated pain. Collectively, HK2 promotes meniscal senescence and OA progression through a non‐metabolic, MYH10‐dependent mechanism, and purpurin represents a promising lead compound for disease‐modifying osteoarthritis drug (DMOAD) development.

candidates.title: Rapid Identification of H3N2 Influenza A Virus HA-Targeting Antibody Epitopes Driven by Computational Antibody Similarity Measures
candidates.authors: Zhu Z, Chen Z, Wu J, Han J, Li L, Qian K, Cui Y, Li Z, Ding R, Pang S, Zhang G, Yu C, Chi X.
candidates.abstract: Antibodies are important therapeutic agents for the prevention and treatment of influenza, and hemagglutinin (HA) serves as the primary target for the development of therapeutic antibodies. However, the identification of epitopes remains an unmet need in the development of such therapeutic antibodies. This study investigates the characteristics of antibody–HA binding interfaces (i.e., epitopes and paratopes) through a computational analysis of all antibody–HA complexes with nonredundant experimentally determined structures from SAbDab, the largest reported antibody structure data set to date. After experimentally identifying and selecting H3N2 HA-specific binding antibodies, a reference antibody library was established. For anti-H3N2 HA antibodies with unknown structures, epitope grouping was conducted based on competitive binding assays that assess interference with the binding of antibodies from the reference library. Based on the complementary relationship between epitope and paratope structures, we selected the structure-based similarity measure most relevant to epitope convergence. Furthermore, we prioritized the experimental validation of binding interference between candidate antibodies and their most structurally similar reference antibodies. We present an integrated computational and experimental framework. This approach includes the construction of an H3N2-specific reference antibody set, computational modeling of antibodies, measurement of antibody similarity, and is complemented by antibody competition binding assays. The dry–wet iterative protocol presented here yielded accurate assessment of the neutralizing potency and breadth of the previously uncharacterized antibody P2A10. Together, the presented pipeline offers a powerful approach for identifying epitopes on anti-H3N2 HA antibodies and for epitope-targeted antibody discovery, while demonstrating the effectiveness of structural analytics in reducing experimental labor.

candidates.authors: Pearce A, Crocetti L, Xu Q, Catarzi F, Guerrini G, Shi Z, Rossi A, Harper A, Ishola A, Abdelrahman S, Patel Y, Huang X, Selleri S, Giovannoni M, Cilibrizzi A, Ladds G.
candidates.abstract: In this study, we employed an extensive drug repurposing strategy to identify new and improved adenosine receptor (AR) antagonists, with the aim of uncovering alternative therapeutic applications for existing polycyclic drug-like molecules. The compounds selected from our library were initially tested using the NanoBRET assay, and the top hits were then subjected to a predictive molecular modeling study, which enabled us to guide the design of new adenosine A1 and A3 receptor (A1R/A3R) antagonists. This approach led to the identification of two lead candidates, which exhibit a different profile of affinity and selectivity toward the A1R and A3R subtypes, attributable to their specific structural features. candidates.title: Simulating Directed Evolution In Silico with an Iterative, Physics-Based Workflow
candidates.abstract: Directed evolution consistently delivers engineered enzymes that facilitate diverse biocatalytic transformations. Despite advances in automation and high-throughput workflows, our ability to rapidly engineer novel enzymes is limited by our inability to thoroughly sample the vast protein design space. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) methods have alleviated this challenge to some degree, due to their ability to propose mutations based on learned patterns from complex protein data sets. However, the hidden logic of these AI-based methods can complicate our ability to reveal and exploit fundamental details of these enzymes. To complement these hidden-logic models, we present a structure- and physics-based workflow that mimics directed evolution in silico. This Virtual Protein EngineeR (referred to as ViPER) aims to simulate directed evolution by leveraging computational modeling, molecular dynamics simulations, in silico mutagenesis, and structure-based property evaluation to iteratively engineer an enzyme toward a desired target. In this work, we present a retrospective analysis to demonstrate ViPER’s ability to efficiently navigate the complex protein–protein interfaces associated with the oligomerization of a ketoreductase (KRED) enzyme. In addition to successfully predicting >70% of sites that are crucial for toggling the oligomerization of this KRED enzyme (after only five rounds), this dynamics-based methodology identifies a distal mutation that was incorporated during experiment-based directed evolution. This work provides a novel foundation for computationally driven directed evolution efforts, opening the opportunity to simultaneously pursue and evaluate multiple evolutionary routes through a physics-based lens.

candidates.title: Targeting the MLN64/STARD3-cholesterol axis disrupts tight junction remodelling and attenuates gastric cancer aggressiveness
candidates.authors: Li A, Chen Y, Zhuang X, Alshammari L, Khan E, Dou Q, Martin T, Jiang W.
candidates.abstract: IntroductionGastric cancer remains a major cause of cancer-related mortality, largely due to invasion, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance. Dysregulated cholesterol metabolism is increasingly recognised as a driver of gastric cancer progression, but how intracellular cholesterol trafficking contributes to malignant junctional remodelling remains poorly understood. MLN64/STARD3 is a cholesterol-binding lipid transfer protein associated with cancer progression, yet its functional role in gastric cancer cell architecture and aggressiveness has not been fully defined. MethodsIn this study, we investigated whether MLN64 is associated with cholesterol-dependent tight junction organisation and malignant behaviour in gastric cancer cells. MLN64 depletion was also associated with reduced ZO-1 protein abundance, disrupted junctional ZO-1 localisation, and impaired tight junction integrity, including reduced transepithelial resistance, altered impedance, and increased paracellular permeability. Functional validation showed that these agents phenocopied several effects of MLN64 depletion, including altered cholesterol distribution, reduced junctional ZO-1 organisation, impaired adhesion/migration dynamics, and reduced barrier function. candidates.title: Tyrosinase–SWCNT Electrochemical Biosensor for Tyramine Detection: Experimental Development and Molecular Dynamics Insights
candidates.authors: Mas’od N, Bahari M, Azhari S, Misral N, Jamali M, Syamila M.
candidates.abstract: AbstractTyramine (TYM) serves as a critical indicator of microbial spoilage and significant health risks at elevated concentrations. Herein, we report an integrated experimental and computational approach to develop a high-performance electrochemical biosensor for selective TYM detection. Tyrosinase (Tyro) was immobilized onto carboxylated single-walled carbon nanotube-modified screen-printed carbon electrodes (Tyro–COOH-SWCNT/SPCE) to construct a nanostructured bioelectrode. The atomistic simulations of Tyro reveal a copper-stabilized binding pocket that accommodates TYM through predominantly hydrophobic interactions. Molecular mechanics Poisson–Boltzmann surface area (MMPBSA) analysis yields a favorable binding free energy (ΔG = −22.46 ± 2.26 kcal mol–1), while per-residue decomposition identifies key histidine and valine residues near the binuclear copper center as major contributors to binding. candidates.authors: Chen L, Chen J, Li C, Jiang L, Liu Y.
candidates.abstract: Nur77 (NR4A1) is an orphan nuclear receptor whose allosteric mechanism departs fundamentally from that of classical nuclear receptors. Using NMR spectroscopy, we identified two conformational substates defined by a pocket enclosed by the H1–H3 loop of the ligand-binding domain. These substates interconvert slowly beyond the NMR detection timescale, reflecting a substantial free energy barrier. Solvent-induced isotope shift (SIIS) experiments reveal differential hydrophobic exposure of these two substates, with the minor substate displaying enhanced solvent accessibility. Integrating multiple sequence alignment (MSA) with mutational dissection, we identified a network of long-range weak interactions that acts as a cryptic allosteric hub governing substate equilibrium. Notably, the two substates exhibit distinct ligand-binding affinities, implying functional specialization. Therefore, this study reveals a non-classical allosteric framework of Nur77, providing a structural basis for the design of drugs that target allosteric regulation.

candidates.title: Deep Learning for Protein Secondary-Structure Segmentation in Intermediate-Resolution Cryo-EM Maps: A Resolution-Stratified Benchmark Dataset and Controlled Evaluation
candidates.abstract: Accurate segmentation of protein secondary structures in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) maps is crucial for protein tracing and atomic model building, yet remains challenging at intermediate resolutions. Although deep learning architectures have recently been applied to this task, there remains a lack of standardized evaluation protocols and systematic resolution-stratified analyses. Consequently, it remains unclear how segmentation performance varies across finer resolution ranges within the intermediate-resolution regime and how different volumetric segmentation architectures compare under controlled experimental conditions. To address these gaps, we present a nonredundant, resolution-stratified benchmark dataset and a controlled evaluation framework for protein secondary-structure segmentation in intermediate-resolution cryo-EM maps. The dataset comprises 972 nonredundant protein-chain samples from 495 cryo-EM protein structures resolved at 4.5–8.0 Å, with voxel-level annotations for helices, sheets, and non-periodic secondary-structure (NPSS) regions. The dataset is stratified into three resolution ranges4.5–5.5, 5.5–6.5, and 6.5–8.0 Åto enable systematic analysis of resolution-dependent segmentation performance. Using this benchmark, we evaluate five representative convolutional and transformer-based volumetric segmentation architecturesU-Net, Residual U-Net, Attention U-Net, UNETR, and Swin-UNETRunder standardized preprocessing, training, and evaluation protocols. Residual U-Net achieves the highest macro-averaged foreground (Macro-FG) F1 score in all three resolution bins, while helices are segmented more accurately than sheets and NPSS regions. All five architectures achieve their highest Macro-FG F1 scores in the highest-resolution bin, whereas performance varies between the two lower-resolution bins across architectures and secondary-structure classes. Overall, this benchmark enables fine-grained analysis of resolution-dependent segmentation performance, supports reproducible method development, and facilitates controlled comparison of future cryo-EM secondary-structure segmentation approaches.

candidates.abstract: Abstract The nucleolus is a key cellular compartment responsible for the major steps of ribosomal subunit biogenesis. Detailed characterization of the nucleolar proteome is essential for understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying ribosome biogenesis and may help identify novel regulators of this process. However, the nucleolar proteome, and the protein composition of early ribosomal subunit precursors in particular, remain poorly defined, largely because of the methodological inconsistencies and conflicting findings across published studies. Here, we aimed to establish a standardized approach that could be used to identify novel factors involved in the early stages of ribosome biogenesis using an optimized stepwise nucleolar extraction protocol, followed by sucrose density gradient fractionation and mass spectrometry analysis. This optimized approach allowed us to enrich for proteins directly engaged in early biogenesis steps, while depleting non-specific nucleolar “background” components. A total of 529 unique proteins were identified across two biological replicates. Gene Ontology (GO) analysis revealed significant enrichment of proteins annotated as ribosome biogenesis factors, including those directly involved in ribosomal subunit assembly and rRNA processing. A cross-referencing of our dataset against 188 known components of pre-ribosomal complexes represented in the PDB yielded 84 overlapping proteins. Early biogenesis factors prevailed in this group (70 out of 84), supporting the idea of the enrichment of the analyzed fraction with early pre-ribosomal complexes. The resulting protein dataset will facilitate the identification of novel factors governing the poorly understood aspects of human ribosome biogenesis. Keywords: nucleolus, ribosome biogenesis, nucleolar extraction, proteomic analysis

candidates.title: Schisandrin B attenuates ischemic acute kidney injury in a CTR1-dependent manner by inhibiting cuproptosis
candidates.journal: Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology
candidates.authors: Lin L, He S, Yang X, Zheng L, Tan W, Li K, Yang J.
candidates.abstract: AbstractBackgroundAcute kidney injury (AKI) remains a global health challenge with high mortality rates and no targeted pharmacotherapy. Although regulated cell death (RCD) drives renal tubular epithelial cell (RTEC) injury, the involvement of cuproptosis, a copper-triggered RCD characterized by lipoylated protein aggregation and iron-sulfur cluster loss, remains unexplored in acute kidney injury (AKI).MethodsIntegrated single-cell transcriptomics (GSE180420), a human renal biopsy cohort (n = 22), ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) mouse models, and hypoxia-reoxygenation (H/R) cellular models were used to characterize cuproptosis. Multi-omics profiling, molecular docking, and CTR1 (encoded by SLC31A1)-specific siRNA knockdown were used to explore the mechanism of action of Schisandrin B (SchB).ResultsSingle-cell RNA sequencing of murine ischemia–reperfusion (I/R) kidneys revealed that cuproptosis was a predominant RCD modality, accounting for approximately one-third of all regulated cell death events in renal tubular epithelial cells (RTECs). This finding was corroborated in human AKI biopsies and in murine I/R kidneys, where the key cuproptosis proteins ferredoxin 1 (FDX1) and copper transporter 1 (CTR1) were markedly upregulated, accompanied by significant copper accumulation and tubule injury. Under the tested conditions, SchB exhibited protective effects at least comparable to those of the classical copper chelator tetrathiomolybdate (TTM) in attenuating copper-dependent cytotoxicity in vitro. SchB-regulated differentially expressed genes were significantly enriched in glutathione metabolism, p53 signaling, cellular senescence, and PI3K-Akt pathways. Molecular docking predicted a direct interaction between SchB and CTR1 (binding energy −5.1 kcal/mol)siRNA-mediated depletion of CTR1 partially abolished the protective effects of SchB against copper-induced RTEC death, indicating that CTR1 may be required, at least in part, for SchB-induced cytoprotection in RTECs.ConclusionThis study identifies cuproptosis as a predominant and previously unrecognized RCD pathway in ischemic AKI. SchB inhibits cuproptosis in a CTR1-dependent manner. These findings provide a preclinical rationale for further investigation of this natural product as a potential therapeutic candidate for ischemic kidney disease.Keywords: acute kidney injury, cuproptosis, oxidative stress, Schisandrin B, SLC31A1/CTR1

candidates.title: Spatial mechanopriming of multicellular interfaces drives cytoskeletal-to-nuclear remodeling to boost therapeutic efficacy of stem cells
candidates.authors: Bayaraa O, Lee N, Kim S, Lee H, Li C, Fu X, Hyun J, Choi G, Choy J, Kim H, Kim H.
candidates.abstract: AbstractEngineering multicellular constructs through biophysical cues, independent of soluble biochemical factors, is a promising strategy to boost the therapeutic potential of stem cells for regenerative medicine. However, the mechanisms by which spatially organized cell-cell and cell-matrix interfaces govern multicellular signaling and subsequent behavioral outcomes remain poorly understood. Here, we elucidate these mechanistic events by introducing 2D nanoplates (∼350 nm) compartmentalized within the intercellular space of mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) spheroids to form de novo cell-matrix spatial interfaces. These interfaces redistribute internal stress across the spheroid, amplifying integrin-cytoskeleton-nucleus force transmission and restoring YAP-dependent mechanotransduction to achieve spatial mechanopriming. Cells within these mechanoprimed spheroids exhibit profound nuclear deformation, epigenetic remodeling, and spatially patterned metabolic activation. Finite element modeling and spatial transcriptomic analyses further reveal a spheroid-wide reorganization of cytoskeletal and transcriptional networks. Mechanistically, elevated cytoskeletal tension across the reorganized interfaces is associated with a putative, tension-associated pseudo-hypoxic signature involving HIF-1α-related signaling, establishing a mechanometabolic niche that robustly enhances angiogenic secretion. Consequently, mechanoprimed spheroids demonstrate superior engraftment, accelerated vascular regeneration, and improved perfusion recovery in a murine ischemia model. Collectively, this work establishes spatial mechanopriming as an effective strategy to remodel cytoskeletal-to-nuclear mechanics and enhance the therapeutic potential of 3D multicellular systems.Keywords: Mechanopriming, Multicellular spheroids, Spatial microenvironment, Nuclear remodeling, Stem cell therapy

candidates.title: The CYFIP2 Arg87Cys Mutation Reshapes the Interactome and Alters Stress Fiber-Associated Proteins
candidates.authors: V. Biembengut Í, Andreassa E, D. M. dos Santos M, Silva I, U. Kurt L, Shigunov P, Carvalho P, de Souza T.
candidates.abstract: AbstractThe Arg87Cys mutation in CYFIP2 has been implicated in early-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE), yet its molecular consequences remain incompletely understood. CYFIP2 functions as part of the WAVE regulatory complex (WRC), where it plays a key role in actin filament polymerization and interacts with RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) to regulate mRNA translation. Previous studies have demonstrated that this mutation alters the structure of CYFIP2, resulting in a gain of function in the WRC. Additionally, the mutation appears to promote the formation of intracellular granules that colocalize with RBPs; however, the impacts of this mutation on these interactions remain unclear. Here, we combined cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) and label-free quantitative proteomics to investigate how this mutation alters the protein interactome and actin regulatory pathways. XL-MS data revealed exclusive cross-links between actin and tropomyosin isoforms in the Arg87Cys variant, suggesting altered cytoskeletal dynamics. Quantitative proteomic analysis of patient-derived neural progenitor cells corroborated these findings by revealing an increase in the abundance of stress-fiber-associated proteins. Altogether, our results point to a broader impact of CYFIP2 mutations on cytoskeletal organization and protein interaction networks with potential implications beyond the nervous system. This is the first study to our knowledge to suggest a link between the Arg87Cys mutation and dysregulation of stress-fiber-related proteins, indicating possible disruption of other actin-processing pathways.

candidates.title: pdb2reaction: End-to-End Reaction-Path Elucidation from PDB Structures Using Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials
candidates.abstract: Elucidating enzymatic reaction mechanisms requires a sequence of computational tasks comprising active-site extraction, minimum-energy-path search, transition-state (TS) refinement, intrinsic reaction coordinate (IRC) validation, and quasi-rigid-rotor harmonic-oscillator (QRRHO) thermochemistrystages typically connected by ad hoc scripting and per-system tuning. We present pdb2reaction, an open-source Python command-line toolkit that automates this entire pipeline directly from a user-curated PDB using a single machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP) backend. A GPU-accelerated pysisyphus fork is bundled to perform the Hessian-based heavy computationsHessian, IRC, and vibrational analysison the same CUDA device as the MLIP for the default backend, minimizing data transfer overhead. This toolkit also implements a bond-change-driven recursive path-search algorithm, which recovered the two-step reaction mechanism of the geranyl pyrophosphate C6-methyltransferase BezAan SN2-like methyl transfer followed by glutamate-mediated deprotonation via a cationic intermediatelocating both transition states and the intermediate itself without a user-supplied intermediate geometry: from a reactant-state active-site cluster and a minimal scan list, and independently from the reactant and product structures alone. On a benchmark of 23 reaction steps across six enzymes, the broadest-coverage backend, UMA-m-1.1, reproduced the literature mechanism for 19 steps, each with a single imaginary frequency at the transition state. For BezA, all five backends recovered the same two-step pathway and the same rate-limiting step. pdb2reaction enables rapid PDB-to-mechanism elucidation on a single GPU, providing a high-throughput complement to higher-cost DFT-based cluster-model calculations and full enzyme–solvent QM/MM calculations.
